query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an unmodified α + β dual-phase alloy whose low hardness and poor friction and wear properties limit its use under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could improve its hardness and wear resistance without sacrificing its existing beneficial properties. State the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, applicable operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A sequential treatment that first deep cryogenically refines the TC4 alloy’s bulk microstructure and then applies a tailored micro-arc oxidation (MAO) coating combined with subsequent laser surface texturing (LST) will synergistically enhance surface hardness and wear resistance without compromising the alloy’s inherent ductility and fatigue properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Unmodified TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloy with its typical α + β dual-phase microstructure and moderate baseline hardness, ductility, and wear resistance.
generation.intervention: First perform a deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) under controlled conditions (e.g., submersion in liquid nitrogen for an optimized duration below 24 hours) to induce phase transformation (increased α' martensite, grain refinement, and higher dislocation density). Then subject the DCT-treated alloy to a micro-arc oxidation (MAO) process in a silicate-phosphate mixed electrolyte to form a dense ceramic oxide layer, and follow this with laser surface texturing (LST) to form controlled microfeatures that enhance coating adhesion and reduce effective contact area.
generation.conditions: The MAO process is conducted at moderate voltages in an electrolyte chosen to yield a dual-layer coating (a thin dense inner barrier and a porous outer layer) while the LST parameters (laser fluence, pulse duration) are optimized so that texturing does not induce coating spallation; tests should be performed under ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and under cyclic high-contact load conditions typical of aerospace or high-service tribological applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The subsurface microstructure refined by DCT (with enhanced martensitic content and dislocation density) acts as a tough, hard substrate, while the MAO-generated oxide layer provides a wear-resistant, chemically inert barrier. The laser-induced microtextures mediate stress distribution and capture wear debris, thereby reducing friction and mitigating crack initiation at the coating–substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: DCT induces martensitic transformation and grain refinement which increases hardness and yield strength without drastic loss of ductility. The subsequent MAO produces a ceramic TiO2-rich coating that acts as a protective barrier from abrasion, and the superimposed laser texturing reduces effective contact area and improves load distribution. This combination is expected to synergize the benefits of enhanced substrate strength and a resilient, patterned oxide coating, ensuring improved wear resistance while preserving fatigue performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated TC4, the composite treatment is predicted to yield a significant increase in surface hardness (potentially on the order of an additional 30–40% based on DCT effects) and a notable reduction (e.g., >20–30% lower) in wear rate and friction coefficient under high-contact-stress conditions, while maintaining or even slightly improving fatigue resistance.
generation.baseline: Unmodified TC4 alloy and single-treatment variants (either DCT-only or MAO+LST-only) serve as baselines.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions of extreme service, including high cyclic loads and contact stresses typical of aerospace or heavy-duty mechanical applications, where maintaining fatigue life and bulk ductility is as essential as surface hardness and wear resistance.
generation.uncertainty: While individual benefits of DCT (PMC11433462::web::017::3_3_1_comparison_of_hardness) and of MAO with laser texturing (PMC11926383::web::023::conclusion) have been demonstrated, the combined synergistic effects on coating adhesion and long-term durability under fatigue are untested. It is uncertain how the modified substrate-coating interface will perform under cyclic loading and whether the texturing parameters can be optimized to avoid spallation, as has been an issue in nitriding plus texturing studies (PMC6356806::web::016::3_3_frictional_properties).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of TC4 samples: (1) untreated control, (2) samples receiving only one of the treatments (either DCT only or MAO+LST only), and (3) samples receiving the combined DCT followed by MAO+LST. Subject all groups to standardized tribological tests (e.g., ball-on-disc wear tests under high cyclic loads) as well as fatigue tests simulating service conditions. Microhardness, coating adhesion (via scratch tests), friction coefficient, wear volume, and fatigue life should be quantified.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or wear volume)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined treatment group does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least 20% reduction in wear rate and a 30–40% increase in surface hardness relative to untreated samples) while maintaining at least comparable fatigue life (within 10% of control) compared to the baseline single-treatment groups, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The reasons why the microhardness of the TC4 titanium alloy base material improved with DCT are mainly the following. Firstly, phase transformation occurred with DCT, the β phase transformed into the α′ needle-like martensite phase, and the relative surface hardness of α′ needle-like martensite played a strengthening role. Secondly, the internal stress generated by DCT inside the TC4 titanium alloy caused an improvement in dislocation density, leading to a corresponding increase in the interaction between dislocations and resulting in a hardening effect. The third reason is that DCT has a refining effect on the grain size. An increase in grain size means an increase in grain boundaries, which can hinder the movement of dislocations and increase the deformation resistance of a material. These macroscopic mechanical properties manifest as an improvement in hardness. However, when the DCT reaches 24 h, there is a certain degree of decrease in the hardness. The LST treatment of the TC4 surface combined with a hybrid electrolyte was employed to enhance the performance of the MAO coating and elucidate its mechanisms for wear reduction and resistance. The main findings are summarized as follows: The MAO coating formed on the surface of TC4 alloy consists primarily of Rutile TiO₂ and Anatase TiO₂ phases.The use of a silicate-phosphate mixed electrolyte facilitated the growth of a coating with a thickness of up to 23.82 μm. The pores within the coating were uniformly distributed, with diameters of approximately 5–6 μm. The coating exhibited a dual-coating structure, consisting of a dense oxide coating (~ 1 μm) in direct contact with the substrate and a loose, porous coating on the surface.The LST treatment of the TC4 surface increased the specific surface area and bonding area of substrate, thereby enhancing the adhesion strength between the MAO coating and the substrate.The LST treatment reduced the average friction coefficient of the MAO coating on TC4 from 0.54 to 0.30, representing a decrease of approximately 44.4%. However, at the high temperatures of 900 and 950 °C, the wear resistance of N + T is superior than that of N. This is because both the hardness and brittleness of the nitrided layer on the titanium alloy increases with the increase of nitriding temperature. When the nitriding temperature is lower, the hardness is improved but the wear debris is relatively less. Thus, the wear volume decreases with the increase of the nitriding temperature. However, when the nitriding temperature is 950 °C, the abrasive wear caused by the spalling hard abrasive debris is more serious, which increases the wear volume. In addition, N + T decreases the surface contact area, which results in the increase of contact stress. When nitriding temperature is lower (750–850 °C), the nitride layer is thinner and the hardness is lower. In addition, the texture increases the contact stress.
